steps.body: A product is a resized copy of one of its factors. 3/4 × 8 takes 8 and scales it by 3/4. Since 3/4 is less than 1, the result is a shrunk version of 8 — so 3/4 × 8 is less than 8. You can tell the size just by looking at the scaler.

widget.prompt: Without computing: is 3/4 × 8 more than 8, less than 8, or equal to 8?

options.label: Less than 8
options.feedback: Right — 3/4 is under 1, so it scales 8 down. The product is less than 8.

options.label: More than 8
options.feedback: Scaling by a number under 1 shrinks. 3/4 < 1, so 3/4 × 8 is less than 8.

options.label: Equal to 8
options.feedback: Only scaling by 1 keeps it equal. 3/4 is under 1, so the product is smaller than 8.

hints: So the product is less than 8.
explanationVariants: Scaling 8 by less than 1 makes it smaller.
Scaling 9 by more than 1 makes it bigger.

widget.prompt: Is 5/3 × 9 more than 9, less than 9, or equal to 9?

options.label: More than 9
options.feedback: Right — 5/3 is over 1, so it scales 9 up. The product is more than 9.

options.label: Less than 9
options.feedback: 5/3 is over 1, so it grows 9, not shrinks it. Less would need a scaler under 1.

options.label: Equal to 9
options.feedback: Only scaling by 1 keeps it equal. 5/3 is over 1, so the product is more than 9.

hints: So the product is more than 9.

steps.body: This lets you compare two products at a glance. 2/3 × 10 scales 10 down (2/3 < 1), while 5/4 × 10 scales it up (5/4 > 1). So 5/4 × 10 is the bigger one — you know it without working either out. The scaler decides the order.

explanationVariants: The over-1 scaler gives the bigger product.

options.feedback: Right — 5/4 is over 1 (grows 10) while 2/3 is under 1 (shrinks it), so 5/4 × 10 is bigger.
2/3 is under 1, so it shrinks 10 below 10; 5/4 grows it above 10. 5/4 × 10 is bigger.

options.label: They're equal
options.feedback: The scalers differ — one under 1, one over 1 — so the products differ. 5/4 × 10 is bigger.

predict.prompt: 4/3 is the scaler. Before building it — will 4/3 × 6 land above 6, below 6, or exactly on 6?

options.label: Above 6 — 4/3 is more than one whole
Below 6 — multiplying by a fraction always shrinks

predict.reveal: “Multiplying by a fraction shrinks it” is only true for fractions BELOW one whole. 4/3 reaches past the whole-mark, so it stretches 6 rather than shrinking it — which the bar is about to show.

widget.prompt: Build 4/3 and watch where it lands against one whole — that comparison decides the answer.

commonFractions.feedback: 3/4 stops short of the whole-mark — that is a scaler that SHRINKS, and it would pull 6 down to 4.5. The numerator and denominator are the other way round here.
One whole leaves 6 exactly where it was. 4/3 reaches past that mark, which is why the product climbs above 6.

widget.lowFeedback: Not yet at 4/3 — keep adding thirds and watch for the whole-mark.
widget.highFeedback: Past 4/3 now — come back down, but stay beyond the whole-mark.
widget.successFeedback: 4/3 crosses the whole-mark — one whole plus one more third. A scaler bigger than one whole stretches what it multiplies, so 4/3 × 6 climbs to 8. The rule is not “multiplying makes things bigger” or “fractions make things smaller”; it is whether the scaler sits above or below one whole.

hints: So the product is more than 6.
explanationVariants: Scaling 6 by more than 1 makes it bigger.
With the same factor, the biggest scaler wins.

widget.prompt: Which product is the largest: 1/2 × 20, 3/4 × 20, or 5/4 × 20?

options.feedback: Right — 5/4 is the only scaler over 1, so it alone grows 20; the others shrink it.
3/4 is under 1, so it shrinks 20. 5/4 is over 1 and grows it — that's the largest.
1/2 shrinks 20 the most. The largest comes from the biggest scaler, 5/4.

hints: Same 20 each time — compare the scalers.

explanationVariants: 7/6 × 12 grows 12 (7/6 > 1); 3/5 × 12 shrinks it — so 7/6 × 12 is bigger.
The over-1 scaler gives the bigger product.

widget.prompt: Both products start with 12. Without finding either product, which scaler makes the greater result?

options.feedback: Right — 7/6 is over 1 (grows 12) while 3/5 is under 1 (shrinks it), so 7/6 × 12 is bigger.
3/5 is under 1, so it shrinks 12; 7/6 grows it. 7/6 × 12 is bigger.

options.label: They're equal
options.feedback: The scalers differ — one under 1, one over 1 — so the products differ. 7/6 × 12 is bigger.

takeaways: A product is one factor scaled by the other — read its size off the scaler.
Scaler under 1 → product smaller than the factor; over 1 → bigger; exactly 1 → equal.
Compare or order products by their scalers, without computing.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **A product is a scaled copy of one factor — check the other factor against 1.** 2/5 × 10 scales 10 by 2/5, and 2/5 is under 1, so the product is less than 10. No need to compute — the scaler tells you.

explanationVariants: 2/5 is under 1, so 2/5 × 10 is less than 10.
A scaler under 1 shrinks the factor.

widget.prompt: Is 2/5 × 10 more than 10, less than 10, or equal to 10?

options.label: Less than 10
options.feedback: Right — 2/5 is under 1, so it scales 10 down. The product is less than 10.

options.label: More than 10
options.feedback: 2/5 is under 1, so it shrinks 10. More would need a scaler over 1.

options.label: Equal to 10
options.feedback: 2/5 isn't 1, so it changes 10 — it scales down, less than 10.
